intent: Implement a capability when a real requirement asks for it, never on the strength of a prediction — so no speculative generality survives into production.
problem: Presumptive features are built, reviewed and tested for a need that never arrives; the effort is wasted and, worse, the guess stays in the codebase as a permanent, slightly wrong complication that every later reader and every refactoring must work around.
context: Applies to any extension point, configuration option, abstraction or feature that exists only because someone forecast a future requirement. YAGNI is inseparable from refactoring: it is only safe where the code can be changed cheaply when the real requirement arrives, so it is a claim about the team's ability to refactor, not a licence to neglect design. Non-negotiable exception cases (internationalisation, compliance, multi-tenancy) are not speculation when the requirement is already committed.
benefits: No effort spent on features nobody asked for.
No speculative 'guesses' left in the code to mislead readers or block refactoring.
Shorter feedback loops: the next real requirement ships sooner.
Less surface to test, document, secure and maintain.
Designs stay honest about what the domain currently needs.
tradeoffs: Missed opportunity when a requirement arrives and the retrofit is expensive — the classic "we would have shipped a month sooner".
Requires refactoring, unit tests and continuous integration to be genuinely present; without them YAGNI becomes technical debt (Jeffries).
Creates organisational friction against product owners who want optionality on the roadmap.
When the prediction is a legal or regulatory deadline rather than a feature, YAGNI is simply wrong.
Repeated late insertion can destabilise a design that was kept deliberately simple.
quality_attributes_note: extensibility 4 is the deliberate trade. security 8 because removing unused surface removes unused attack surface — speculative endpoints and options are frequently forgotten by hardening passes.

participants.responsibility: The committed requirement that authorises implementation.
participants.notes: Ron Jeffries' formulation: always implement things when you actually need them, never when you just foresee that you need them.

participants.responsibility: The speculative need; its only effect should be to change priority, never to create code.
participants.notes: The counterfactual ("usually what you actually need is quite different") is why guessing pays so badly.

participants.responsibility: The safety net that makes deferral affordable.
participants.notes: Without continuous refactoring and automated tests, YAGNI is not applicable.

use_cases: Not building a plugin interface until a second plugin exists.
Not adding a generic <T extends Entity> repository when only one entity type is persisted.
Removing an unused "for future scaling" sharding layer from a single-node deployment.
Not building an i18n framework before the second locale is required (i18n retrofits are the documented exception when already committed).
Dropping an unused multi-channel notification strategy with one channel.
avoid_when: The requirement is a committed external constraint (regulation, contract, hardware spec, security baseline).
The architecture is a published extension point other teams already depend on.
The change is genuinely expensive to defer (a data format others consume, a wire protocol, a public API).
There is no refactoring capability — no tests, no CI — so deferral becomes accumulation.
The "speculative" feature is a non-functional requirement (observability, auditability) that cannot be retrofitted without downtime.
pitfalls: YAGNI used as an argument against fixing the internal quality of code that already exists (Fowler explicitly rejects this).
Genuine requirements being reclassified as speculation when they are merely inconvenient.
Building the extension point but not the feature, leaving dead structure behind — the worst of both.
Citing YAGNI to reject a non-functional requirement (audit logging, rate limiting) that only matters at scale.
Deferral without a recorded trigger, so nobody ever comes back.

related_patterns_notes.kiss-principle: KISS constrains the shape of a design you are building; YAGNI constrains whether you build it at all.
related_patterns_notes.rule-of-three: Rule of Three is YAGNI's structural corollary: do not build the general mechanism before the third case exists.

anti_patterns: Configuration switches for behaviour no deployment enables.
Generic base classes or plugin registries with a single implementation.
Abstract methods left unimplemented with a "not needed yet" comment.
Flexible schema columns typed as "any" awaiting an unforeseen use.
A framework shipped to "prove the architecture" before the product exists.
design_principles: Always implement things when you actually need them, never when you just foresee that you need them (Ron Jeffries, Extreme Programming).
Do the simplest thing that could possibly work (DTSTTCPW) — the XP practice YAGNI underwrites.
Yagni is not a justification for neglecting the health of your code base; Yagni requires (and enables) malleable code (Martin Fowler).
Even if you are totally sure you will need a feature later, don't implement it now (Cunningham & Cunningham).
best_practices: Ship the simplest thing that satisfies the current story, then refactor when the next story arrives.
Keep continuous integration, automated tests and relentless refactoring in place, or YAGNI is unsafe.
Record the prediction in the backlog instead of the codebase.
Deliberately build flexibility only where refactoring is measurably expensive.
Review each new configuration option: which deployment sets it?
